topic: Why you normally cannot see your own rapid eye movements in a mirror
centralQuestion: Why does direct mirror perception omit rapid eye motion that can be seen in later playback?
thesis: Understand how simultaneous looking and moving, rapid retinal motion, reduced sensitivity and visual masking differ from watching a recording afterward.
viewerPayoff: Understand how simultaneous looking and moving, rapid retinal motion, reduced sensitivity and visual masking differ from watching a recording afterward.

visualOpportunities.title: One person and one mirror
visualOpportunities.description: Over-shoulder person at a framed mirror; two reflected eyes and gaze targets. Push toward eyes while subjective state is clearly labeled. No third-person view falsely frozen. Camera icon beside same mirror portrait, then visibly transition to later playback with a moving iris. Recorded external view, not direct mirror perception. Macro eyes show a brief ballistic movement then a labeled slowed replay revealing continuous rotation, no teleportation presented as physical fact. Pull back to shoulder and reflection, highlight that reflected eyes and observer are the same person. Optical link stays continuous. Same eye pivots in simplified side section; light from a fixed mirror feature falls on changing retinal positions. Not a detailed neural circuit. Carry eye and retinal sweep into a softly attenuated feature illustration; qualitative dip spans before/during/after, never a flat zero or blackout. Same eye closeup expands into before/blur/after sequence, then clear flank views visually dominate. Label perception schematic, time expanded. First-person mirror view shifts gaze target and resolves without black frames; stable perception illustration, not literal subjective recording or complete explanation of spatial constancy. Large camera/playback frame shows filmed iris moving while a small stationary viewer-eye motif establishes steady current gaze. Replay timeline distinct from original recording. Return to original person/mirror with continuous reflected movement on external view; momentary direct-perception annotation and confident resolved ending.
